In the heart of a lively soccer field, Ivy succumbs to a fatal poisoned drink, leaving suspects Meredith and Hugo to face the relentless inquiries of Detective Winston.

Winston walked his fingers over the glossy crime scene photos spread out before him. The soccer field, typically a place of good-hearted competition and family fun, had been turned into a spectacle of horror as Ivy met her untimely end. The only saving grace was that the game had been called off before the tragedy unfolded.

Ivy was a frequent attendee of these games, often seen happily sipping on a cold drink from the stand. This time, it had been her undoing.

Winston was no rookie, but cases like these sent a cold shiver up his spine. Putting the photos back into the case file, it was time to pay Hugo a visit. 

Hugo was perched on a stool in the recording booth when Winston arrived. Despite the match being called off, Hugo had been working as a sound engineer at the same match. His work as a sound engineer was only a few blocks away from the matchplex, it was a stone throw away. Working with sound engineering also meant that Hugo had to handle chemicals regularly as part of his job role. Winston noticed a tattoo peeking from the arms of Hugo's rolled-up flannel – the name Anna, inked with what seemed like a real sense of devotion.

"Hugo?" Winston asked, leaning against the doorframe.

"That's me," Hugo replied, his eyes never leaving the windows of his booth.

"I hear you were serving refreshments at the match yesterday," Winston said, trying to keep his tone neutral.

"I was, yeah," Hugo confirmed with a nod, "I often help out there."

"You've been seen leaving work that day, "Winston continued.

"Yeah, I left to go set up the refreshments," Hugo responded.

At first glance, Hugo didn’t seem like the type who would care about a toxicology course, but records indicated he had taken one in the past. Moreover, his work required him to handle complex sound equipment which could involve frequent contact with certain chemicals.

Winston circled back to Hugo's protective side. "You seem close to Anna."

"Yeah," Hugo’s gaze softened, "hee, she's like my baby sister. I've always looked out for her."

Any detective worth his salt knew how protective bonds could drive people to extreme lengths. Winston had heard from others about some cruel remarks Ivy made about ruining Anna and of threats to press charges against her. 

"All right Hugo," Winston said, throwing his coat over his arm, "thank you for your time."

Winston had more pieces to the puzzle now, but he knew the killer wouldn't reveal himself easily. Winston, as always, would be waiting patiently. After all, a game of cat and mouse was half the thrill of his job.

Winston's latest case had piqued his curiosity, leading him to a popular coffee shop downtown where Ivy, the person of interest, was a regular. As he strolled in, the distinct aroma of dark roasted beans permeated the air. Behind the counter, Meredith worked with great efficiency amidst the morning rush. 

"Ivy was a regular here?" Winston questioned and Meredith nodded. "Every morning, like clockwork. Black coffee, a splash of half-and-half. No sugar,” she described Ivy's drink preference.

From a nearby television, a clip replayed on the local news – Ivy, laughing boister⟦ously⟧ whilst imitating some sacred rituals, unmistakenly disrespecting Meredith's beliefs. Winston looked towards Meredith, who now busied herself with a new order – an infusion of a variety of substances readily on hand: chocolate shavings, cinnamon sprinkles, and an endless assortment of flavored syrups.

"Do you mix all the drinks?" Winston asked. Meredith, too preoccupied, responded with a nod. Every shift, Winston noted, Meredith would arrive donning religious symbols around her neck. Today was no exception. As she prepared for her work day, her fingers grazed her amulets and she muttered a silent prayer before diving into the morning pandemonium.

Meredith often spoke publicly about being a staunch follower of her religion and openly declared – more times than Winston would care to count – that anyone who disrespects her beliefs deserves severe punishment.

Right when the morning rush started to wear off, Meredith slipped into the backroom, tugging off her apron. Winston’s eyes landed on a bag near the entrance - a familiar logo from the local butcher shop from where she regularly purchased raw meat.

In the midst of the bustling shop, Winston's attention was drawn to a framed photograph. Meredith was captured mid-spit, a chicken wing in hand.

"But she only buys raw meat," the butcher's words echoed in his mind, contrary to the image he was witnessing. He recalled Meredith’s friends' words: "Meredith has never had cooked meat in front of us."

With lunchtime approaching, the crowd began to ebb and Winston found a moment to delve deeper. In a passing query, he asked, "Heard about the news? Ivy, laughing at your beliefs - that was caught on camera."

Meredith’s hands clenched a coffee cup so tightly it overflowed. In her eyes burned recognition and some suppressed pain. She merely muttered how disrespectful Ivy was.

A customer chimed in, ordering a highly customized drink and Winston’s observation heightened as he watched Meredith expertly mask all traces of the various ingredients she used in the drink. A craft eerily similar to certain practices of subterfuge.

As Winston reached out to accept his coffee—an all-black with a splash of half and half, he pondered over the peculiar pieces of the jig-saw. His goodbye was met with a cautionary note from Meredith, "Hey detective, respect every belief you come across... seems like the world could use more of that, you know?”

As Winston stepped onto the sidewalk, Meredith’s words left him with a chilling twist in his investigation.<turn|>

In the shimmering depths of a popular scuba diving site, Julian's life was brutally extinguished with a crowbar; now, it's up to Detective Winston to dive into the murky secrets of suspects Lucy and Clara.

While examining the photos from the murder scene, Detective Winston couldn't help but feel a chill crawl up his spine. Beneath the bubbles, the crime scene lay at the bottom of the ocean, a place that was supposed to be a sanctuary for divers like Julian. 

His train of thought was interrupted by his partner who handed him a pile of interview transcripts and surveillance files to go through. He was about to dive into the world of their main suspect, Clara.

Coming from a workstation that was perpetually cluttered with stacks of serial killer novels, Clara no doubt had a keen interest in the subject matter. She was frequently engrossed in conversations about infamous serial killers, delving into their modus operandi with unsettling accuracy without any need for references. During her lunch breaks, she could always be found pouring over one of her many true crime books.

Clara, a skilled metal worker, had a specific niche in crafting a variety of unique crowbars, which had become her signature work. Her craftsmanship was distinct and always earned her respect amongst her peers. Going through a surveillance tape, he watched as Clara loaded her uniquely crafted crowbar into her vehicle before heading out to the diving site. The crowbar didn't seem out of place, what with her being a metal worker and competitively acknowledged for her unique metalwork.

Her performance at work had been nothing short of outstanding, and she had been putting in long, overtime hours. She was highly dedicated to her work and never missed an opportunity to express her ambition for a promotion.

Julian and Clara both worked at the same company, and both had been in the running for the same promotion. During the office water cooler chats, he'd heard Clara express her keen interest in the promotion, and her evident disappointment when Julian became a potential contender.

The evidence was laid in front of him: a woman with an enthusiastic interest in killers,⟦ always⟧ reading her crime books even on her lunch breaks, a craftsman with a signature touch on uniquely crafted crowbars, and seen with one on the day of Julian's infamous dive. A metal worker who had been putting in long hours for an impressive performance. All that tied with the delicate balance of coworkers both competing for the same promotion. 

One piece of evidence caught his eye. Clara was also a part of the diving team on the day Julian was murdered. With that, Winston pushed back his chair, stood up, and prepared to pay Clara a visit. He had a feeling there would be more to dig up from her perpetually stacked workspace, files and statements during her interrogation.

Winston stood overlooking the gentle sway of the ocean, the sun reflecting a glaring path of light towards the spot where Julian's body had been found. The dive was a secluded affair, intended just for a small, close-knit group of divers which included Lucy and Julian, often dive partners.

Derailing his thoughts, he flicked through his notes, focusing on Lucy's background - the woman had a varied history, from construction sites to docks, her hand attending to many trades. She'd even taken a boat maintenance course somewhere along the way. A crowbar tool was commonly used in both professions. 

"Detective Winston, Miss Lucy is ready to see you," a uniformed officer approached him. 

"Thank you, officer," he responded, shaking his head in dismissal, his eyes still on the open files in his hand.

He walked into the impromptu interview room, eyes finding Lucy easily. She looked out of place in the cold, steel-colored room, her complexion still holding on to the sun-kissed hue from the sail.

"Lucy," Winston began, his tone neutral. "You and Julian. I've been told you two dive together frequently," he watched her face for any signs of reaction.

"Yes," she confirmed curtly. "Julian and I...we were friends," she added before a tight swallow. "He betrayed my trust though, caused me significant trouble."

That drew his attention. He decided to delve into the more intimate details, "You were managing the tools for this trip?"

Caught off guard, Lucy straightened. "Yes...yes, that's correct. I've always taken care of the gear, packed the crowbar too. Just a precaution..."

"I see. Just a precaution," he repeated.

Catching her eye, he questioned further, "Lucy, did you overhear Julian discussing this betrayal?"

A flicker of shock passed over her face. "Yes...with someone I didn't recognize," she admitted. 

Another clue. He asked, "Lucy, did you find any evidence in Julian's belongings?"

"I... I found some documents in his gear locker...which I always thought only I could access," she confessed.

"Interesting. Very interesting," he nodded before standing up, preparing to leave but not before confirming one last detail.

"You shared the same boat, is that correct?" 

"Yes," Lucy admitted, looking rather bewildered by the question. 

"Very well," said Winston, concluding his interview and leaving Lucy to her thoughts, his mind buzzing with the new information and the unfolding mystery.<turn|>

In the chilling silence of a hockey rink, Marvin's life was brutally ended with a machete,⟦ leaving⟧ Detective Winston with two elusive suspects: Justin and Frederick.

Detective Winston made his way through the bustling crowds at the local hockey rink. The place had a distinct, chilling atmosphere today, the murder of Marvin casting a grim shadow over it.

He spotted Justin not too far away, watching the game with a fixed expression. Justin had been noticeably depressed since a particular event - he had once proposed to Marvin's fiancé, expressing his undying love, only to be mercilessly rejected. After this incident, he was never quite the same, living with a constant air of despair and refusal to engage with happiness.

"Justin," Winston called out, making his way over. As soon as Justin heard the detective's approach and caught sight of the man in uniform, his eyes instantly lit up, always eager to gain more information about the crime.

"Detective," Justin greeted, his expression somber, yet subtly eager, "here for the game or here about the recent crime?"

Winston raised a brow. Justin seemed too interested. "Any hockey fan would be here for the game," he replied, "Marvin was going to play, wasn't he?"

Justin's dry eyes took on a spark when the murder was mentioned again. He looked dejected at the mention of Marvin, but nodded, "Yeah, he was. I was here to watch it." He had been with the crowd entering the hockey rink at the time of the murder, ready for the game and totally unprepared for the tragedy that eventually unfolded.

He paused, glancing around the rink, then asked, "Do you know how they got in? The murderer, I mean."

Winston kept his expression unreadable, but he noted Justin's quick change of topic back to the crime. "Through the main entrance," he stated simply, "like anyone else," he added, reaffirming that Justin had entered the same way.

"And the time... when exactly did it happen?" Justin changed the topic right back to the crime again, the flame in his eyes burning brighter at the prospect of new details.

Winston frowned slightly, "During the game," he answered, watching Justin's face carefully. He appeared unphased.

Justin cocked a brow, excitement mixed with intrigue evident in his lit eyes. "I was here during that time," he pointed out, "Watching the game."

Winston nodded, "You were, and as far as anyone knows, you didn't leave until well after," he almost sighed, "Listen Justin, what exactly is it with you and this crime? It seems that you're more interested in it than the hockey game."

Justin shifted, looking anywhere but at him, "Well, it's just...Marvin and his fiancé, you know. I just thought they...weren't right for each other. I had a talk with her once. I asked her not to marry him. But she didn't listen."

A sudden clang of a puck hitting the net caught their attention, but Winston kept his gaze on Justin, watching, and listening. There was a lot more to this case than meets the eye, he knew. However, his interview with Justin had just ended, leaving him with more questions than answers.

The harsh, industrial lighting of the hockey rink painted a grave picture as Detective Winston surveyed the crime scene. The rink's security tapes corroborated Frederick's presence at the scene, even capturing a heated argument between him and Marvin. In this particular argument, Marvin was heard threatening harm to Frederick's defenceless daughter. Frederick, a curator of a local weapons museum, also held a job at the hockey rink, giving him a valid reason for being there.

Setting that evidence aside, Winston trotted towards the museum, a place Frederick frequented due to his love for antique machetes. Frederick had the responsibility of overseeing the unique collection of blades, his dedication emanating as bright as the lights above the collection.

What piqued Winston's interest though was that one of the machetes in Frederick's collection matched the description of the weapon that ended Marvin's life. Such violent usage of a machete aligned with Marvin's previous harmful behavior; aggressive threats and unbidden visits to the girls' locker room only added to the growing list of his offensive conduct. After obtaining the necessary legal papers, Winston re-examined the machetes, concluding the lethal weapon indeed came from Frederick's collection.

Taking a break from the museum, Detective Winston investigated Frederick further by questioning those who knew him. His protective behavior for his daughter was a common topic, supported further by a chilling detail given by a coworker in the hockey rink's locker rooms.

"Marvin once threatened Frederick's girl. Frederick didn't take it lightly, and they've been arguing ever since," the coworker confessed. Despite the locker rooms being an area exclusively accessed by staff with keys, Marvin had been spotted in there more times than anyone could count.

Winston's sharp gasp caught the coworkers attention, "What is it, Detective?"

"Nothing...just...let me know if you notice anything else...odd," replied Winston.

Echoes off the old lockers were the only responses he got.

With a cluttered mind flooded with information, Winston had a lot of thinking to do, miles to go before this case could be put to rest.<turn|>

When Isolde is found savagely killed with barbed wire in her home office, Detective Winston must untangle a web of lies and deception to find out if Samuel or Bernard is responsible.

Winston's nose wrinkled as he entered a home office that had been marred with blood and remnants of barbed wire. Whispers of Isolde's last moments — what had she seen, what had she felt — clung to the air, making Winston's skin cling to the white collar of his shirt. 

A key piece of Isolde's life had been her role in exposing medical malpractice. Video evidence, meticulously collected, strangely presented itself beyond the crime scene. She had been building a case against Samuel, a man Winston was becoming increasingly interested in. 

Samuel had been a paramedic, receiving intense training which even included handling emergency situations with injuries from barbed wire. The unfortunate ironic nature of his education was not lost on Winston. He was a man trained to save lives, to handle emergencies. But there had been a serious error during a previous medical procedure, an error Samuel found hard to live down. Now, he made his living in a medical supply store, trying to make up for lost time, perhaps. 

One sunny Monday, Winston himself had seen Samuel, sunglasses shading his eyes, his job posing no hindrance to his apparent penchant for intrigue. Just the next day, the sunglasses had been replaced with eyeglasses. That was a curious detail — Samuel didn't have a prescription for eyewear.

Intriguing, things left to ponder. 

As for the barbed wire, that vile instrument's origin led back to a storage unit. Samuel had a key to said unit. Had he known about its contents? It was, after all, not a common item for city dwellers to come by. 

Then, there was the matter of the hair. Samuel, a typical brown-haired man, had recently been seen sporting hair as dark as the night. A local store clerk had mentioned selling black hair dye to a man fitting Samuel's description days prior. 

Winston remembered mutterings of a superior warning Samuel about potential job loss even jail time. The detective felt a chill run down his spine as he processed the connections. 

A visit to Samuel was in order. 

Similar to sirens he responded to, Samuel generated a certain kind of alarm in Winston's mind too. It was time to figure out who was saving lives and who was ending them. Perhaps, sometimes, they were one and the same, Winston couldn't help but consider as he headed to interview the paramedic, and potential suspect, Samuel.

Winston was a weathered detective who had seen it all, or so he thought, until he was handed his latest case - the murder of Isolde. The crime scene was none other than her shared home office with her partner, Bernard. The fatal weapon, strangely ominous, was a strand of barbed wire.

After hearing the details and evidence, Winston found himself interviewing Bernard, the primary suspect and Isolde's live-in partner. Bernard resided a far distance from the oftentimes chaotic city that Winston had become accustomed to. He owned a sizable cattle ranch, his pride and joy, and importantly, his primary source of income. 

Upon entering the shared living space of Bernard and Isolde, Winston could not help but notice the peculiar co-existence of their realities. The cattle rancher, strong and rugged, cohabiting with Isolde, a woman known for her tight grip over critical territories in the criminal underworld. These territories not only had huge implications for their income but also facilitated their criminal endeavors. 

"Bernard," Winston began in his calm, measured tone, "Can you account for your whereabouts on the night of Isolde's murder?" 

"I was here. Alone," Bernard slowly responded, his words echoing the stark emptiness of their shared home. His only alibi appeared to be his isolated ranch.

Winston was aware of one crucial information piece; Bernard's regular grumbles about Isolde's monopoly over the crime territories. A monopoly Bernard would have liked to gain control of, no less. "There seemed to be persistent disagreement between you and Isolde over these territories, is that right Bernard?" 

Bernard chuckled deeply, "It's simple, detective. In our line of work, we all want more territory, it directly influences our business."

Glancing across⟦ the⟧ ranch, Winston's gaze fell on the fences that lacked their usual barbed wire adornment. "Seems like you're short on barbed wire," he said.

"Needed it for a fence repair. Got distracted before I could finish," Bernard replied nonchalantly. 

"But isn't it odd that nobody else in town reported any missing barbed wire?" 

Bernard gave no response, his eyes offering a contrasting silence to the glaring sun. As Winston prepared to leave, he couldn't shake off the feeling that there was more to this story. Bernard was alone at the moment of Isolde's reported murder, with no visitors reported during the time of the crime, and his own sprawling ranch as the only possible alibi. His suspicions deepened by the fact that Bernard had had a clear motive - the lure of control over vast crime territories.<turn|>

On a night when the roar of go-karts was silenced by a nefarious deed, Detective Winston finds himself investigating the peculiar murder of Gary, slain by a rarely-seen sai with two unlikely suspects: Frederick and Jerome.

Detective Winston flicked through the reports once again. The guy is a dock worker, moved shipping containers around all day. It was a harmless hobby, but it didn't sit right.

"The dock's a rough place, Winston," said Officer Daniels, a baby-faced officer with a knack of not following orders, "You can't be weak and thrive there."

"I bet Frederick's co-workers would tell you about his strength and dexterity. Cargo isn't a walk in the park," Winston said, taking in Daniels' recommendation. Strength and dexterity... it reminded him of something. The weapon, a sai, was found in Frederick's collection.

Winston rubbed his brow lightly and continued turning the pages. Frederick was a devotee of warfare artifacts. From ancient katana to modern assault rifles, Frederick had them all. 

"Frederick goes for racing during his free time," the report read. In fact, suspicious activity at the go-kart track was often reported around Frederick's usual racing time. Winston remembered Frederick's racing schedule: every Thursday at six, without fail.

On the day Gary was killed, Frederick and Gary were both at the go-kart track. Gary, a joker at heart, was seen messing around with Frederick's go-kart, the very same one that Frederick had previously confronted others about.

Winston sighed, leaning back in his chair. Daniels had a defensive glance in his eye.

"But he's just an enthusiast! And skilled, I heard," Daniels defended, almost pleadingly. 

Winston only nodded, his mind already spinning with strategies and weak alibis. 

"He's also a dockworker, known for his strength and dexterity, able to handle heavy cargo safely." He paused. "Isn't a sai a pretty lightweight weapon?"

"Yes sir." Daniels stuttered out, not daring to look Winston in the eye. "Frederick..." he swallowed. "Frederick might have the skill to wield a sai."

Winston continued reviewing the reports and evidence, his mind far from eased, his heart heavy with the task at hand. The dockworker. The go-kart track. The sai. The confrontations over the go-kart. The timelines adding up just so... Suspicions were nothing until proven in the court of law. But still, it was a start. Time to pay Frederick a visit.

Clouds hovered above the go-kart track as Winston surveyed the murder scene. The sight of Gary's lifeless body had been replaced by yellow police tape, but the stain of what had occurred remained imprinted in Winston's mind.

Indisputably, Gary was the current go-kart champion of their small town. A title that endowed him a sense of invincibility and an obstacle for Jerome, the runner up more times than Jerome cared to admit.

Winston pulled the collar of his coat up, glancing around the track at the groups of people, all huddled up and whispering.⟦ Among⟧ the crowd, his eyes locked onto a man standing alone, pressing binoculars to his eyes. It was a quirk of Jerome's to carry binoculars, even to social gatherings. The man was Jerome, a local driving instructor.

As Winston approached, he saw numerous people trying to engage with Jerome. He seemed to be in his own world, unresponsive to those attempting to speak with him. His attention constantly straying elsewhere, ears tilted towards passing conversations as if eavesdropping. Winston couldn’t help but notice the insular behavior of the man.

"You're Jerome, right?" Winston asked. The man gave him a nod, his gaze fixed on the distant track. Jerome's listless eyes betrayed not apathy but a high passion for go-karting.

Jerome and Gary shared this passion, Winston learned, their go-kart rivalry was quite the spectacle in the local area. Contentious races, frequently ending with Gary taking the championship title very heatedly debated, and it was just a week ago when Gary accused Jerome of cheating.

"In his own world, isn't he?" commented one of the local racers, watching Winston's attempt to engage Jerome. "I've heard them arguing a lot recently. Especially after the last race..." he glanced at the silent Jerome.

Winston noted to visit the local gym, where Jerome had been seen practicing fight moves occasionally. The man was known to have a certificate of martial arts mastery as well. That singled him out, especially considering the nature of the murder weapon, a sai.

Thinking of sai, a cold wave of realization spread through him. He had seen a receipt in Jerome's office for multiple such weapons, and rumor had it that Jerome had been spotted purchasing multiple sais only a week back.

As the evening wind picked up, Winston took one last look at the solitary figure of Jerome. He was engrossed in his own world even in a crowded gathering. Suspicion, it would seem, wore many masks. It was time, Winston decided, to uncover the truth.<turn|>

In the heart of a bustling fitness center, Heidi's life was abruptly silenced by a shotgun's blast; now it's up to the astute Detective Winston to round up suspects Grace and Chester and unravel the threads of this complex murder mystery.

Winston studied Grace's appearance as she labored over the dismantling of her shotgun, a routine she performed with a kind of measured grace that only came with practice.

"I take it hunting is a regular hobby of yours, Grace?" he asked. She straightened her back and brushed a lock of hair from her eyes, her hands still loosely holding the dismantled firearm. She nodded.

"It's tradition. Heidi and I would always go out into the wilderness, me with my nine-two shotgun, her with her ridiculous tin of marshmallows. I remember she'd always be the one who'd leave, while I'd stay at the fire, peering into the forest, not returning to the tent." Grace chuckled, but her smile didn't reach her eyes. "Even when we were out here, pushing fitness, she was looking out for safety."

"And you had a mutual workout routine both of you followed?" Winston questioned.

"Yes, every day like clockwork." She sighed. "But I convinced Heidi to change it. I argued it was safer, better for her. That night she was murdered, she implemented the change."

Winston looked at her, his sharp eyes noticing the glimmers of distress in hers. "Could that change have caused her to meet her killer?"

"She started seeing someone. I thought it was best if we changed the time, to throw off this new person. But she didn't listen..." Her voice held a slight edge, possessive almost.

As she related the details about her trips with Heidi, Winston noticed her rain-soaked hiking boots, mud-streaked pants, and her tired eyes.

"Looks like you've been out there yourself today?" he gestured at her appearance.

"Busy day," Grace responded curtly, her gaze never leaving the shotgun she was now starting to reassemble. "I usually got up the earliest. Not much point in sleeping when there's hunting to be done. The guys in the camp aren't morning people anyway."

"I see," Winston muttered, "You two, you worked out together frequently, didn't you?" 

"Heidi's the one who introduced me to working out at the fitness center. We would even do so late at night, just us, a lot of sweat and a hell of a lot of heavy lifting." She smiled at the thought, her eyes glossing over with a mixture of remembrance and grief. 

Winston nodded, scribbled down a few lines in his notepad and thanked her for her time. There was still so much to understand, so much to link together.

Sunlight filtered in through the windows of the fitness center, casting long shadows on the equipment and machines scattered around the vast room. In the corner of the spacious gym, Chester was spotted, tending to some weights when detective Winston walked in.

Chester, slight in stature, belied his physical prowess as a jockey. His wiry exterior seemed incongruent with the voracious power emanated by his presence. "Hello Chester," Winston began, his gruff voice noticeably contrasting with the calmness of the gym.

"Detective Winston, isn't it?" Chester replied with ease, his demeanor not showing a single shred of surprise or fear. Just two weeks ago, Chester had started⟦ his⟧ new gig at the fitness center, partly to make some extra bucks and partly to maintain his fitness routine. It wasn't surprising to Winston that Chester would frequently show up right when Heidi, an active member of the gym, was last seen alive.

Just when he had started to become regular at the gym, murmurs among Chester's gang had grown louder. They've started questioning his loyalties, not convinced that his regular visits to the gym were purely for maintaining his fitness.  

Their subtle talk was interrupted by the loud reverberations of gunshots in the distant background. Chester, an avid hunter, often flexed his shooting skills at the range nearby after winding up work at the gym.

"You like to shoot, huh?" Winston casually pointed towards the direction of the gun shot sounds. "Yeah. Helps take the edge off," Chester replied, a faint smile appeasing his otherwise-hardened face.

The conversation gradually led them to Heidi, a brave woman who had recently made criticisms about Chester's gang at a local town meeting. Their illegal activities were an open secret in town, countered only by the fear they instilled in those who dared to oppose. Heidi was the latest in the list, her fate tying in with an unfortunate coincidence: Chester's gang members are known to carry shotguns, the same kind that ended her life. 

Detective Winston and Chester finally diverged to their respective routines. The detective's mind was buzzing with theories, but his face was an ocean of calm. He had gathered the facts. The story had to be spun. His job could not be influenced by hasty conclusions... not when the facts all led to one presumable as intimidating as Chester.<turn|>

Detective Winston regarded the lone figure sitting before him across the table. Richard’s face was absorbed in the glow of the paused true crime documentary, his eyes reflecting morbid fascination and intense concentration.

"Just finishing up your work-out?" Winston asked, gesturing towards the sweat-soaked shirt.

Quite challenging to get the swings right. Purchased these nunchaku from a sports equipment store last month. It's part of my martial arts training."

"Martial arts? I wouldn’t have expected that from a waiter," Winston said, conversing readily.

"The mosque I work at, it's next to this martial arts institution. We do nunchaku⟦ training⟧ as part of our drills. Isabella, tragically enough, was also a part of the same class, and I just like keeping myself engaged." Richard shrugged.

"Speaking of keeping engaged," Winston glanced towards the paused documentary on the laptop, "Looks like you've got quite the fascination with true crime, huh?"

"I listen, rewind, analyze, and repeat..." Richard said, reaching towards his notebook that lay next to the computer, brimming with his own investigation strategies, "I write down interesting details. I find it... intriguing, to say the least."

"Ah, a keen observer. Useful in a job like yours," Winston said, nodding in understanding. 

"I rarely interact with anyone outside my working hours, detective," Richard asserted with a hint of defensiveness, immediately finishing off his sentence. "The day the tragedy happened, I was at the martial arts class first, then I went to the mosque...but I was alone."

"So, you're a mechanic apprentice, right?" Winston asked. "You work with these kinds of tools every day?"

Addison looked at him for a moment before nodding. "That's right. It's my field of work. Handling tools like crowbars is just part of the job."

Winston left Addison with his book and his workshop, making his way out to his car.

Camping, tool handling, busy campgrounds... Winston had a lot to think about on the drive back to the station. But, as always, the detective knew better than to rush to any conclusions just yet. He also knew that she had picked up a knack for handling construction tools, crowbars included, from her watch in the building business.

"Officer Octavia," started Winston, trying to appear casual, "Officer 'tavia," he corrected himself, as per the way locals referred to her, "you were on patrol the night Ernest was murdered, correct?"

Her gaze remained steady, not threatening nor hesitant, "Yes, that would be right."

"Were the campgrounds along your route?" asked Winston, knowing that he was treading on thin ice. The campgrounds which were part of her regular beat were also where poor Ernest was found dead.

"They sure were," she replied without diverting her gaze. "I've patrolled there for years now."

Winston pressed on, “Ernest, a known revealer of secrets, was threatening to leak his current findings. He'd uncovered an officer’s shady past and he claimed it was yours. Know anything about that?”

Octavia just looked through him, her facial muscles taut as she remained stoic. "Ernest was always digging around for information, but I can't say I do."

Staying strategic, he continued, "Ernest indicated that this officer with supposed shady practices was involved in illegal activities before joining the force. Oddly reminiscent of your own construction and police career, Octavia. Fearful of any skeletons in the closet that might be found?”
